options.author: first read (Wonder)
options.case: - The gap between Taki's cherished, unwritten inner work and the squalid, absorbing business that actually fills his days — and the way the narration keeps lending the second the epic language of the first. Taki is a writer who has not really begun: he tells his wife the work is 'about half' done (p28) when in fact, once he took up his pen, he could write it 'in one burst' at any time — or so he believes; putting it into prose feels to him as clumsy and roundabout as making conversation. Everything grand in the story stays in his head, in quotation marks. Everything that actually happens is petty and physical: a pond dug for no good reason, carp that cannot be caught, a house about to be demolished and replaced by a warehouse, a telephone he suddenly decides to sell, carp suddenly worth four hundred yen, creditors at the door. The story's energy is the traffic between the two. His wife's casual remark that his finished seascape looks 'like a snowscape, in midsummer' (p58) detonates a paragraph of self-laceration in which all his realistic fiction and his whole foolish way of living become a botched 'snowscape', a blizzard rises, and he must flee across a white wilderness (p61–62). By section III the same man is bellowing orders at two workmen in a muddy pond like a general, then like an impresario inviting spectators up to the best seats, then discovering that this is more fun than any pleasure he knows (p165–179). In section IV the pumping-out of the pond, done by his assembled creditors, acquires 'the same underlying force as the chorus of Nancy Lee' (p210) — the sentimental whaling song he inherited from his father — while Taki himself is simply absent, gone to Tokyo 'to buy a lamp' (p212). If a translation resolves this into satire on a lazy writer, or into lyrical sympathy for a dreamer, it has chosen one pole and lost the story. For the English: Keep the comic disproportion intact. Do not make Taki's inner language beautiful and the pond business merely coarse background, and do not make the narration wink at him from outside. The same English must be able to inflate a carp-hunt into a battle, a chorus, a theatrical tableau, and then let it collapse into mud, cicadas and an unpaid bill. His quoted-back phrases — “the difficult work I'm holding in my head!”, “in one burst!”, “Nancy Lee”, “the telephone!”, “the terrifying blizzard!”, “nothing but a snowscape to look at!” — should recur recognisably, because in p160 the narration throws his own slogans back at him as they all scatter 'like goose down' while he sits glaring at the pond.
options.tradeoff: One crux, broadly framed: it preserves both poles and forbids a verdict, but gives no specific instruction on the workmen's vernacular or Taki's imitation of it.

options.author: crux check (Wonder)
options.case:
- TAKI SEES THE WORLD IN REVERSE SEASON: HIS 'FINISHED' SUMMER SEASCAPE LOOKS — RIGHTLY — LIKE A SNOWSCAPE, BECAUSE HE LIVES IN AN UNWRITTEN, 'HELD-IN-THE-HEAD' FANTASY AND IS BLIND TO WHAT IS IN FRONT OF HIM. THE WIFE'S CASUAL LINE IN p58 TRIGGERS NOT EMBARRASSMENT BUT A FULL MID-SUMMER BLIZZARD HALLUCINATION IN p61-62 (OWL'S EYES IN DAYLIGHT, BURIED UNDER SIN-FUL SNOW 'AS LARGE AS PEONY PETALS'). THE SAME WORDS KEEP RECURRING — 架空 MADE OF AIR, 夢, 'IN ONE BREATH' (p28, p74-75), THE SIX-DAY JOB HE MUST ONLY 'HOLD IN HIS HEAD' (p135, p160) — AND IN p160 THE NARRATOR LISTS THEM BACK VERBATIM TO SHOW THEM ALL SCATTERED 'LIKE GOOSE DOWN' THE MOMENT MONEY APPEARS. THAT MAKES THE TITLE AN INDICTMENT, NOT A MOOD. For the English: KEEP THE SNOW LITERAL, SUDDEN AND UNEXPLAINED, AND KEEP A RIGID CONCORDANCE FOR THE REPEATED PHRASES — 'in one breath/at one go,' 'hold it in my head,' 'Nancy Lee,' 'telephone,' 'terrible blizzard,' 'snowscape' — SO THE CATALOGUE IN p160 LANDS AS SELF-QUOTATION. DO NOT SMOOTH THE SUMMER/SNOW INVERSION INTO A SIMILE FOR HIS STATE OF MIND.
- THE COMEDY AND THE VERDICT ARE IN THE COLLISION OF REGISTERS: LYRICAL, MOCK-HEROIC NARRATION OF A MUDDY POND-SIEGE AGAINST THE WORKMEN'S VULGAR DIALECT — AND TAKI, WHO CLAIMED NO FEELING FOR ANYTHING (p18), BECOMES A SHOUTING, TABLE-THUMPING 'GRAND BOURGEOIS' (p160) THE INSTANT THE DESPISED CARP ARE WORTH ¥400. A AND B SPEAK IN HEAVILY ELIDED, ROUGH VERNACULAR (p40-47, WITH THE NARRATOR EVEN GLOSSING 手前え AS 'FIRST PERSON'), AND THEIR BODIES — DRAGON AND UNFINISHED HANNYA TATTOOS (p48) — ARE GIVEN THE EPIC DESCRIPTION TAKI'S OWN WORK NEVER GETS. THE POND BATTLE (p154-193) IS NARRATED AS WARFARE, THEN UNDER-CUT BY 'A WATER-FIGHT ON A HOT DAY.' TAKI FIRST EAVESDROPS, THEN IMITATES A'S CADENCE, ORDERS THE CARP BEATEN TO DEATH (p173), AND BY p210 HIS CREDITORS ARE PUMPING THE POND TO THE RHYTHM OF NANCY LEE'S CHORUS WHILE HE IS ABSENT IN TOKYO BUYING A LAMP. For the English: KEEP THREE REGISTERS SHARPLY APART IN PLAIN, SPEAKABLE ENGLISH: HIS EVASIVE MUMBLE AND FALSE GRANDIOSES, THE WIFE'S BRISK DOMESTIC LOGIC, AND THE WORKMEN'S COARSE, COMPRESSED ROUGH-SPEECH (WITHOUT EYE-DIALECT CARICATURE). ABOVE ALL KEEP TAKI'S SLIDE INTO IMITATION OF A (p165-176) BRUTAL AND COMIC — IT MUST SOUND LIKE A DIFFERENT MAN FROM THE 'SNOWSCAPE' REVERIE, NOT A POLISHED NARRATOR SUMMARISING.
options.tradeoff: Two cruxes, narrowly framed: it adds rigid concordance, literal snow and a distinct register crux, but hardens the story into an indictment/verdict that the other reading expressly forbids.

fork.question: Do they name the same thing in different words, or different things? They overlap on the unwritten-work/pond traffic, the snowscape detonation, the recurring slogans and the Nancy Lee pond scenes, but they are not the same crux restated: Option 0 makes the refusal to judge Taki the crux itself, while Option 1 makes judgement — title as indictment, comedy as verdict — and the three-register collision, including Taki's imitation of the workmen, separate cruxes. Choosing between them decides both the book's tone toward Taki and whether dialect/register is a load-bearing translation rule or a by-product of comic disproportion, and that choice will recur on every page; the text as quoted does not settle it, since the same scenes (p58–62, p160, p165–210) are cited by both sides for opposite tonal conclusions. Recommendation: proceed on Option 0 until the editor rules, because it contains Option 1's evidence without pre-deciding the verdict or a rigid concordance, whereas proceeding on Option 1 would bake a satirical stance and phrase-freezing into the draft that would be expensive to undo if the editor prefers the open reading.

data.say: FORK: The two readers substantially overlap but name different cruxes — Option 0's crux is the unresolved traffic between Taki's unwritten inner work and the petty business that borrows its epic language, with an express bar on resolving it into satire or sympathy; Option 1 adds a second, distinct crux in the collision of three registers and Taki's imitation of the workmen, hardens the snowscape/title into an indictment and a verdict, and imposes rigid concordance. I therefore do not pick: this is not one better than the other, it is a recurring question of tone and of whether register is itself load-bearing, and the scenes both cite (p58–62, p160, p165–210) support either tonal conclusion. I open a fork and recommend the run proceed on Option 0 in the meantime, since it preserves both poles and all the shared evidence without locking in the indictment or the concordance, which would be costly to reverse.
